Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) sensors provide a promising method to assess real-world human motion kinematics.
However, multi-day multi-IMU tracking is difficult due to the desynchronization driven by inaccurate IMU clocks.
In this study, 15 volunteers wore IMUs continuously on their thighs and shanks for 5 weekdays (Mon-Fri), which included 3 repeated in-lab motion capture sessions.
We synchronized thigh and shank IMUs using two methods.

The first was physical calibration, where we maneuvered the IMUs in a rigid holder to produce sync signals pre-donning (Mon) and post-doffing (Fri), then linearly resampled data from one IMU to match the other via cross-correlation.
The second was signal-based periodic updates, where we shifted IMU clocks hourly based on the timewise alignment of preprocessed body-worn acceleration signals.
After syncing, we used sensor-tosegment alignment and accelerometer-gyroscope fusion to estimate knee flexion and compared results to camera-based motion capture.
Physical calibration alone removed clock offset in most cases, where IMU-estimated knee flexion generally matched motion capture (correlation ≥0.944; root-mean-square difference RMSD ≤6.9°).
But in some participants, residual mid-week desynchronization (~0.2s) resulted in misestimated knee flexion (Wed: RMSD up to ~19°).

After applying signal-based updates or combining it with physical calibration, IMU matched motion capture on all 3 days (Mon: r ≥0.975, RMSD ≤6.1°; Wed: r ≥0.971, RMSD ≤6.2°, Fri: r ≥0.977; RMSD ≤5.9°).

Our multi-modal synchronization enables week-long knee flexion tracking and lays a foundation for advanced syncing tools, for improving the feasibility of wearable multi-IMU systems to continuously monitor real-world knee kinematics in clinical studies.
NEE mobility is critical for daily function and longterm joint health.
Conventional assessments of knee kinematics rely on camera-based motion capture in the lab, which do not capture the frequency and variability of habitual movement in daily life.
Wearable inertial measurement units (IMUs) offer a promising alternative by using accelerometer-gyroscope fusion [1], [2] to track segment orientation and joint angles outside the laboratory.

text.text: Recent studies, including our own [3], have shown that IMUs track knee flexion with accuracy comparable to camera-based motion capture during common movements such as gait [1], [4], [5] and stair navigation [6].
text.formatted: Recent studies, including our own <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>, have shown that IMUs track knee flexion with accuracy comparable to camera-based motion capture during common movements such as gait <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> and stair navigation <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6]</ref>.

text.text: However, nearly all such validation studies were performed in a single experimental session, leaving it unclear whether this tracking quality holds after multiple days of continuous recording -the use case that most multi-day IMU monitoring studies require.

Several studies have recorded multi-day IMU data to report cumulative real-world metrics, most commonly step count and activity level [7], [8], [9] and more recently cumulative kinematics like limb elevation duration or body rotation [10], [11], [12].
text.formatted: Several studies have recorded multi-day IMU data to report cumulative real-world metrics, most commonly step count and activity level <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> and more recently cumulative kinematics like limb elevation duration or body rotation <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: A critical technical barrier to extending this work to joint kinematics is inter-sensor synchronization.

Unlike singlesensor metrics, multi-IMU measures like the knee flexion angle -an established biomarker in knee osteoarthritis [13], [14] -require that all sensors share a common, accurate clock, which is difficult to guarantee over multiple days [15].
text.formatted: Unlike singlesensor metrics, multi-IMU measures like the knee flexion angle -an established biomarker in knee osteoarthritis <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> -require that all sensors share a common, accurate clock, which is difficult to guarantee over multiple days <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>.

text.text: Research-grade high-end IMUs can synchronize in real time via wired triggers or radio-frequency signal checks [16], but these constrain sensor placement, shorten battery life, and increase user burden, making them impractical for large multiday studies.

text.text: Lower-cost, unconnected IMUs such as the Axivity AX6 (Axivity Ltd., Newcastle upon Tyne, UK) can log a full week of accelerometer and gyroscope data without recharging, which improves wearer adherence [8], [11] but often sacrifice sensor synchronization features for extended logging capabilities.

text.text: Such low-cost sensors rely on internal quartz clocks that are inaccurate by tens of parts per million [17] -enough for two AX6 units to desynchronize by several seconds per day [15], far exceeding the precision needed to align thigh and shank motion for knee flexion estimation.

text.text: Past studies have addressed this by prescribing wearers to physically maneuver multiple IMUs together to generate a shared calibration signal [11], [12], but participants do not always adhere to these instructions [11].

text.text: A simpler strategy is for research staff to perform this calibration maneuver only at the start and end of the wearing period and resample the data assuming a linear inter-IMU clock drift [17].

text.text: However, this procedure relies on the linearity of sensor clock drift, which is sensitive to acceleration and temperature [17].
text.formatted: However, this procedure relies on the linearity of sensor clock drift, which is sensitive to acceleration and temperature <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, calibration-based strategies are easy to implement in theory but challenging in practice.
Requiring multiple lab visits or relying on participants to perform the sensor synchronization themselves will result in data attrition.
Early sensor stoppage due to battery loss, insufficient memory, and either forgetting or incorrectly performing the maneuver could all disable calibration-based synchronization.
Moreover, nearly all prior multi-day kinematic monitoring has targeted the upper limb or torso [10], [11], [12].
text.formatted: Moreover, nearly all prior multi-day kinematic monitoring has targeted the upper limb or torso <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: To our knowledge, no study has confirmed whether a multi-IMU system can track knee flexion with camera-comparable accuracy across multiple days of continuous wear.

Our goal was therefore to develop simple, reliable postprocessing synchronization methods for low-cost IMUs (specifically, the AX6) to continuously quantify the knee flexion angle over multiple days, with accuracy comparable to camera-based motion capture.

We expected that, after proper synchronization, IMU-estimated knee flexion would show small magnitude differences and strong waveform agreement with camera-based motion capture across clinically relevant activities throughout the entire tracking duration.
II.
text.formatted: <head>II.

text.text: METHODS
text.formatted: METHODS</head>

text.text: We used Axivity AX6 (Axivity Ltd., Newcastle upon Tyne, UK), which is a low-cost (~$250 USD), water-resistant research-grade IMU housed in a compact plastic casing with a micro-USB port for charging and data offload (Fig. 1a).
text.formatted: We used Axivity AX6 (Axivity Ltd., Newcastle upon Tyne, UK), which is a low-cost (~$250 USD), water-resistant research-grade IMU housed in a compact plastic casing with a micro-USB port for charging and data offload (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>).

text.text: At a 100 Hz logging rate with both accelerometer (16g range) and gyroscope (2000 dps range) active, a fully charged AX6 records approximately 7 days of continuous data without wearer interaction, including recharging.
We used these settings (16g, 2000 dps, 100 Hz) for both thigh and shank sensors in all experiments.

For each participant, we programmed the thigh and shank IMUs to begin recording simultaneously at a specified time on the day of their first lab visit (always a Monday), shortly before sensor calibration and attachment.
We recruited 15 healthy young adult volunteers from our local community (8 male, 7 female, 27.1 ± 5.8 years old, body mass index = 24.7 ± 5.8 kg/m²) between September 2025 and March 2026.

Participants had no current or self-reported lower-limb or back injury in the prior 6 months that could interfere with knee movement in daily living and were required to be able and willing to visit our lab 3 times in one week (Monday, Wednesday, Friday) for motion capture and to wear IMUs on their thighs and shanks continuously across this 5-day span.
All participants provided written informed consent.
This study was approved by the University of Pennsylvania Institutional Review Board (Protocol #850424) and performed in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
Sensor attachment.
Each participant's initial visit occurred on a Monday, a mid-week visit that Wednesday, and a final visit that Friday, at approximately the same time each day.
We attached IMUs to both legs on Monday and removed them on Friday.

We secured a total of 4 AX6 IMUs to each participant -one pair per leg, on the lateral mid-thigh and lateral midshank -using a 3-layer medical-grade adhesive system (protective base layer, double-sided bonding tape, and a waterproof cover layer; full product details and application steps in Supplemental Methods S1).

Sensor orientation (charging port down, text facing the skin) was matched across all 4 IMUs, which was necessary for extracting calibration syncing signals (Section E) and sensor-to-segment alignment (Section F).

Participants replaced the outer waterproof cover as needed but did not replace the base or bonding layers; they were instead instructed to abort the experiment if those layers detached, which occurred for only 1 of 15 participants (later re-enrolled for a successful 5-day monitoring period).
For the remaining 14, all sensors stayed at their original locations for the full week.
In-lab motion capture.

After sensor attachment, each participant performed a static pose trial (for sensor-to-segment alignment; Section F) followed by 6 movement trials common to daily living -overground straight walking, improvised arbitrary walking, double-legged squat, stair step-up, stair step-down, and 30-second sit-to-stand -at a self-selected pace, recorded with markerless motion capture [18] (specific movement start/end definitions are provided in Supplemental Table S1).
text.formatted: After sensor attachment, each participant performed a static pose trial (for sensor-to-segment alignment; Section F) followed by 6 movement trials common to daily living -overground straight walking, improvised arbitrary walking, double-legged squat, stair step-up, stair step-down, and 30-second sit-to-stand -at a self-selected pace, recorded with markerless motion capture <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> (specific movement start/end definitions are provided in Supplemental Table <ref type="table">S1</ref>).

text.text: We recorded at least 3 gait cycles of straight walking and 3-5 repetitions of each other trial.
This protocol was repeated on Wednesday and Friday.
After the Friday session, we removed all sensors, performed the end-ofmonitoring physical calibration (Section E), and offloaded the 5-day IMU data.
Participants then completed an exit survey on wearing experience and a diary of notable high-intensity activity during the week (Results are summarized in Appendix A).
Briefly, all 15 participants found the 5-day bilateral wear feasible, and 11/15 (73%) would wear sensors for a full week in future studies.

Our IMU processing pipeline converted thigh and shank accelerometer-gyroscope data into knee flexion angle in 3 steps: inter-sensor synchronization, sensor-to-segment realignment, and accelerometer-gyroscope fusion (Fig. 2).
text.formatted: Our IMU processing pipeline converted thigh and shank accelerometer-gyroscope data into knee flexion angle in 3 steps: inter-sensor synchronization, sensor-to-segment realignment, and accelerometer-gyroscope fusion (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>).

text.text: We performed all data processing using Python 3.11.5.

Although IMUs were worn bilaterally (for a larger ongoing study and for feasibility assessment; Appendix A), we report findings from one leg per participant: the dominant leg for 13 of 15 participants, and the non-dominant leg for the other 2 participants because of sensor recording errors on the dominant leg.
Original time stamps logged by the AX6 were non-uniform.

Therefore, immediately after data import (using the Open Movement Project's Python module [20]), we resampled each accelerometer and gyroscope channel to an exact 100 Hz using cubic spline interpolation (SciPy).
text.formatted: Therefore, immediately after data import (using the Open Movement Project's Python module <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20]</ref>), we resampled each accelerometer and gyroscope channel to an exact 100 Hz using cubic spline interpolation (SciPy).

text.text: We also removed rare highmagnitude transient error signals (observed once, >100× physical range) that would otherwise interfere with downstream processing that references global signal maxima.
text.formatted: We also removed rare highmagnitude transient error signals (observed once, >100× physical range) that would otherwise interfere with downstream processing that references global signal maxima.

text.text: We developed two independent inter-sensor synchronization methods: (1) calibration-based linear resampling, using syncing signals from a physical calibration tool and maneuver performed before and after the wearing period; and (2) signal-based periodic updates, using engineered features from the body-worn acceleration signals themselves.
Both methods began with a shared initial clock alignment, established from the physical calibration signal recorded on Monday.

This initial time synchronization does not impose a meaningful burden on experimental setups because it can be performed at the time of IMU software initialization by the researchers rather than study participants immediately before sensor donning.
Physical calibration tool and initial alignment.

Because AX6 does not synchronize in real time, we designed and 3Dprinted a rigid holder to perform initial time synchronization between the 4 IMUs following established recommendations for physical inter-sensor calibration [15], [16].
text.formatted: Because AX6 does not synchronize in real time, we designed and 3Dprinted a rigid holder to perform initial time synchronization between the 4 IMUs following established recommendations for physical inter-sensor calibration <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref>, <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref>.

text.text: We inserted all 4 IMUs into the holder facing upward (Fig. 1a) -opposite their on-body orientation -so that a distinctive, automatically detectable signal is produced (Fig. 3).
text.formatted: We inserted all 4 IMUs into the holder facing upward (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>) -opposite their on-body orientation -so that a distinctive, automatically detectable signal is produced (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Immediately before the scheduled recording start on Monday, we placed all 4 IMUs into this static "calibration standby" position and left it for at least the first 30 seconds of all recordings, then performed a 3step rest-swing-rest maneuver (lifting and swinging the holder for ~10 s, then resting it again) to produce an isolated syncing signal.
We repeated this procedure on Friday, immediately after doffing sensors from the participant.

We detected each "calibration standby" interval automatically from characteristic accelerometer/gyroscope signatures (full detection criteria in Supplemental Methods S2) and used cross-correlation (SciPy) of the resulting waveforms (Fig. 3) to establish the initial Monday clock alignment, which was used by both synchronization methods below.

text.text: Our goal was to develop simple, reliable post-processing synchronization methods that support continuous monitoring of knee flexion over multiple days using low-cost, unconnected IMUs.

We developed and compared three workflows -physical calibration-based linear resampling, signal-based periodic updates, and a combination of these strategies -on thigh-shank AX6 pairs worn by 15 healthy adults for 5 days.
At the group level, all three workflows produced knee flexion estimates of acceptable accuracy through our previously established kinematic processing pipeline [3].
text.formatted: At the group level, all three workflows produced knee flexion estimates of acceptable accuracy through our previously established kinematic processing pipeline <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref>.

text.text: At the individual level, however, they differed: linear resampling alone produced multiple mid-week outliers, which we traced to non-linear inter-IMU drift that this method cannot correct.
Periodic updates fixed this non-linear drift, and combining the two methods further reduced misidentified or unresolved offsets.
Knee flexion angle results showed strong agreements with concurrent camera-based motion capture regardless of whether periodic updates were applied on linear resampled or the original IMU data.
Our findings therefore generally favor periodic updates over linear resampling, though each method carries its own assumptions and constraints.

More broadly, this 5-day validation extends the tracking quality previously demonstrated only in minute-long sessions to ~100 hours of continuous data, supporting the technical and practical feasibility of multi-day, multi-IMU knee kinematic monitoring in future clinical studies on chronic conditions like knee osteoarthritis.

text.text: However, unlike that report, drift was not always linear in our data (13/15 participants, 87%) and varied by experiment even for the same IMU pair, suggesting AX6 clock behavior is not fully device intrinsic.
Although device age and ambient temperature are both known to affect quartz-oscillator timing accuracy [26], they were similar across our experiments and sensors (relatively new, <4-year-old).

text.text: Rather, the two nonlinear drift events we observed each coincided with a period of unusually vigorous activity reported in the participant's activity diaries (a basketball game and an outdoor run).
This indicates high-acceleration events, not time or temperature, may be the more relevant driving factor of non-linearity.

This observation raises an important caveat for the linearresampling approach: because it assumes constant drift, it may be less reliable for physically active wearers, even as it performed well for other non-outlier participants and on Monday/Friday even for the two outliers (because calibration "anchors" bound the Monday and Friday sessions directly).

Linear resampling may still be preferable in some contexts because it requires no shared motion between adjacent body segments, thus it remains available for bilateral or otherwise unconnected segments.

It may also suit studies with shorter monitoring windows or where sensors can be attached, detached, and recalibrated mid-experiment, since the rigidholder signal is inherently more reliable than cross-correlating each segment's naturally distinct motion.
Linear resampling may be better suited to less physically active populations, such as many patients with knee osteoarthritis, though this requires direct validation.
Periodic updates, by contrast, kept mid-week data synchronized even in the presence of non-linear drift and produced no poor-tracking outliers at the individual level (Fig. 8).

text.text: When combined with linear resampling, 98% of sessions stayed within 0.05 s of synchronization.
Because our periodic update method uses unlabeled body-worn signals rather than prescribed physical action, it is robust and usable even when an end-of-monitoring calibration is missing or invalid.

Also, since it updates forward through the recording, it can still synchronize data up to the point where a sensor stops recording prematurely, a failure mode that would otherwise disable linear resampling entirely.
To our knowledge, this is the first method to synchronize thigh and shank IMUs via their shared general motion-intensity envelope.

It suggests that valid multi-day knee flexion tracking could in principle extend as long as the paired recordings last, supporting the broader feasibility of week-long multi-IMU kinematic monitoring with low-cost, unconnected sensors.

text.text: This means our synchronization methods were able to extend prior single-session validation -typically limited to minutes of data -to continuous tracking across 5 days and to a range of clinically relevant tasks (gait, stair navigation, squat, sit-to-stand).
These findings support our synchronization approach as a practical route to reliable, multi-day IMU kinematic monitoring in patients with chronic knee pathology.

Because our approach minimizes wearer interaction, it may be well suited to clinical populations with lower technology literacy or adherence, but several challenges remain before deployment in clinical monitoring studies.

First, while sensor donning can occur at a clinical visit with the help of researchers, sensor doffing -and the end-of-monitoring physical calibration required for linear resampling -will often need to happen at home before sensors are returned by mail.
This may be difficult for patients with reduced hand dexterity and suggests a need for a more user-friendly calibration hardware.
Second, our hourly periodic updates occasionally misidentified an offset before self-correcting it at the next checkpoint (Fig. 5).
text.formatted: Second, our hourly periodic updates occasionally misidentified an offset before self-correcting it at the next checkpoint (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>).

text.text: This imperfection could transiently bias knee flexion estimates for up to an hour and may be caused by either imperfect active bout selection or incomplete separation of the shared versus segment-specific motion features.
Tuning the frequency of periodic update intervals may help address this weakness.
It also remains to be confirmed whether those shared motion features between thigh and shank remain valid for patients with pathological knee motion patterns.
Third, our results represent the best case in which no sensor was repositioned during the week, which will not always hold in larger studies.

Marking the sensor footprint on the base tape to guide self-reattachment is one practical mitigation strategy, though automatic detection and post-hoc data correction in response to repositioning would be a valuable future addition.
More broadly on the limitations of this study, our synchronization approach was validated only on the AX6.
While we expect similar quartz clock behavior in other unconnected low-cost IMUs, we cannot confirm this directly.
We did not assess frontal-or transverse-plane knee motion, for which we lacked reliable reference data [24].
text.formatted: We did not assess frontal-or transverse-plane knee motion, for which we lacked reliable reference data <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24]</ref>.

text.text: The knee flexion estimate is resilient to gyroscope signal drift, but 3-axis Euler angle decompositions would introduce drift-related errors that are not corrected in absence of a magnetometer.

Recent work by Phan et al. developed novel strategies to account for these drift errors but still found that knee frontal and transverse plane kinematics produced unacceptably high errors compared against ground-truth biplane fluoroscopy [27].
text.formatted: Recent work by Phan et al. developed novel strategies to account for these drift errors but still found that knee frontal and transverse plane kinematics produced unacceptably high errors compared against ground-truth biplane fluoroscopy <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">[27]</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our cohort of healthy young volunteers likely adhered to our athome IMU wearing protocol better than a patient or older population would.
Larger studies in such populations should anticipate more non-adherence and practical issues like skin irritation.

We nonetheless believe continuous, real-world IMU kinematic data is critical for gaining objective and patientspecific insights into how musculoskeletal diseases and treatments affect movement outcomes in patients during realworld scenarios.
Therefore, we encourage continued development of wearable protocols and analytic methods that support multi-day kinematic tracking.
Our study developed a simple and reliable syncing paradigm for low-cost logging IMUs to continuously quantify the knee flexion angle during real-world activities.

We showed that our bimodal algorithm reliably syncs two low-cost IMUs to quantify knee flexion for 5 consecutive days, ~100 uninterrupted hours with comparable accuracy to lab camerabased motion capture.

Our 5-day IMU monitoring strategy is a viable solution for clinical studies because it requires minimal wearer interaction and addresses common challenges of patient monitoring with unsupervised software solutions.
Our novel syncing algorithms support low-cost wearable IMUs like AX6 to be implemented in at-home experiments on a larger scale.

We hope our technical contributions will help expedite the translation of wearable technologies into larger clinical studies, like continuously monitoring multi-day knee kinematics to evaluate how musculoskeletal diseases and treatments affect real-world knee mobility in patients with chronic pathologies like degenerative knee osteoarthritis.

Overview of our workflow to convert thigh and shank IMU data into knee flexion angle.
After initial sync alignment, thigh and shank IMUs were synced by either linear resampling (via physical calibration), periodic updates (via body-worn signals), or a combination of both.
After syncing, alignment and fusion procedures were performed independently on thigh and shank IMUs.
The thigh and shank segment sagittal angles were subtracted at the end to determine the knee flexion angle.

Example of extracted physical calibration sync signals (gyroscope zaxis) after initial alignment and before-after linear resampling.

Moving both IMUs while mounted in the rigid-body holder (Fig 1a) allowed us to capture identical signal waveforms that can be cross-correlated to identify inter-IMU clock offset at the time of the physical calibration. (a) In this example, the two IMU clocks were physically calibrated and aligned on Monday, < 1 min after the recordings started. (b) At 344,665 seconds (~4 full days later, on Friday), the two clocks have desynchronized by 1.26 s, or approximately 0.013 s per hour if assuming a linear clock drift. (c) Resampling data based on linear dilation of the slower clock (shank IMU in this example, red) resynchronized the two IMUs at the time of the end-of-monitoring calibration performed shortly after Friday's in-lab session.

Synchronization quality timewise farther away from initial and final calibration "anchor" timepoints, e.g., on Wednesday, depends on the linearity of the inter-IMU clock drift.
Fig 4.
Example of jerk-based daytime and sleep time parsing.
Black signal line is the denoised and smoothed sum of jerk absolute value used for thresholding.
Thin green horizontal line is the individual-specific threshold.
Yellow shaded areas are identified daytime periods (including partially recorded Monday and Friday); unshaded areas in between are sleep periods.
Our 1-hour, 4-iteration rolling average filter helped distinguish daytime rests (e.g., mid-Mon, mid-Wed) from true sleep periods.
Semitransparent waveforms in the background show normalized resultant accelerations from both IMUs and demonstrate the validity of our daytime parsing algorithm.

The updates, which were larger at the first checkpoint of each day as we expected, kept desynchronization <0.05 s for most of the time.

text.text: Although misidentifications occasionally occurred, they were usually selfcorrected at the next hourly checkpoint (blue arrows).
For context, the black dots illustrate offsets of the same IMU pair identified with no day-night parsing (2), criteria-based bout selection (4), filtering (5), or correction.

A notable non-linear drift occurred (red arrow), which led to residual desynchronization on much of Wednesday when only using linear resampling for syncing (green dashed line = assumed linear drift correction).
There were also substantially more instances of misidentified sync offsets, especially during nighttime (unshaded areas).
Fig 6. (a) Example of a 1-hour update interval, and its criteria-extracted 5-minute sync bout.
Note that signals in the first half of this 1-hour interval were too quiet for cross-correlation.

Only the signals in the 5-minute bout were filtered, for syncing purposes only. (b) Snippet of scaled and 4 Hz low-pass filtered resultant acceleration signals from shank (red) and thigh IMUs (blue) after the clock-shifting synchronization.

While shank and thigh accelerations exhibit distinct waveforms, low-pass filtering attenuated their unique waveform features (indicated by the lower magnitudes after filtering) while preserving their shared general intensity profiles like the speed-up, steady, and slow-down phases of an isolated walking bout.
Our rationale for using the thigh-to-shank crosscorrelation for synchronization was based on such shared general motion intensity envelopes between the shank and thigh.
Both methods effectively removed inter-IMU clock offset.
Across the 45 sessions (15 participants × 3 lab days), periodic updates alone kept residual offset ≤0.03 s in 34 (76%) and ≤0.05 s in 40 (89%) sessions (worst case: 0.11 s, one Friday session).

Linear resampling alone kept residual offset ≤0.03 s in 40 (89%) and ≤0.05 s in 41 (91%) sessions but produced the two largest residual offsets of any verification -0.19 s and 0.18 s, both on Wednesdays.
The other sessions >0.05 s were also on Wednesdays for linear resampling alone.

text.text: Combining linear resampling with periodic updates performed best: 39 (87%) sessions ≤0.03 s and 44 (98%) ≤0.05 s, with only one session (0.08 s, a Wednesday) exceeding 0.05 s.
Fig.7.
Example on the effect of incrementally induced desynchronization on the estimated knee flexion angle, shown on a straight walking trial from one participant.
A ±0.05 s sync offset between the thigh and shank IMUs typically resulted in an 8° -9° knee flexion difference compared to synced data.
To limit potential kinematic inaccuracies under 5°, the inter-IMU sync offset should be controlled within ±0.03 s.
Fig 8.

Example knee flexion angle during straight walking gait cycles from a participant (same one as Fig 5), comparing IMU-based (red) to camera-based estimates (black) on Monday (top), Wednesday (center), and Friday (bottom). (a) Results from data synced by linear resampling only.
IMUs had reasonable accuracy on Monday (RMSD = 7.1°) and achieved minimal difference to camera-based on Friday (RMSD = 4.9°), but agreements were much worse on Wednesday (Rxy = 0.609, RMSD = 16.0°).

This is likely explained by the large residual clock offset (0.19s via our verification) caused by non-linear clock drift and unresolved by linear resampling (Fig 5). (b) Results from data synced by periodic updates only.
Results greatly improved on Wednesday (RMSD = 6.0°) and remained the same on Monday (RMSD = 7.1°).

The marginally worse result on Friday (RMSD = 5.7°) may be due to imperfections in auto-selected sync bouts (Fig.6a), or that the time of this in-lab trial was farther off its last hourly checkpoint (periodic update) than Friday's physical calibration (just minutes after the lab session), which allowed minor desynchronization.
Fig 9.
Group-wise mean (line) ± 1 standard deviation (shade) on IMU-estimated knee flexion (red) versus camera-based motion capture (black) on Monday (top), Wednesday (center), and Friday (bottom).
Data shown was synced using both calibration-based linear resampling and signal-based periodic updates.
Syncing with either linear resampling or periodic updates produced results of similar agreement to the camera-based reference (Supplemental Material: Fig.S1, S2).

However, only using linear resampling led to multiple outlier cases where mid-week tracking errors were substantially worse and unacceptable, likely caused by unresolved nonlinear clock drifts (Fig.8a).
In contrast, data synced by periodic updates did not exhibit such failure (Fig.8b).
